title: Senior Maritime Leadership Personality Assessment
notice: Original draft items; no validated scoring key or equivalence established.

questions.statement: When information remains incomplete, I prefer an early defensible decision to prolonged analysis.
I question long-established operating assumptions even when recent results have been satisfactory.
I become less decisive when commercial expectations conflict with my own assessment of operational risk.
I prefer to retain final control of high-consequence decisions, even when officers are experienced.
An unfavourable outcome rarely makes me doubt a decision that was soundly reasoned at the time.
Several minor warning signals are enough to make me reconsider an otherwise successful plan.
I initially defend my own interpretation when another senior professional challenges it.
I readily accept ownership of outcomes arising from authority I have delegated.
My firsthand vessel experience usually carries more weight than advice from an external specialist.
I ordinarily choose a predictable result over a potentially superior but less certain one.
I find it difficult to abandon a plan after investing significant effort in developing it.
In unfamiliar circumstances, I tend to apply proven judgment patterns before exploring alternatives.
I can accept damage to my reputation when a difficult decision protects long-term interests.
I occasionally continue analysing options after a reasonable course is already apparent.
Clear boundaries of authority matter to me more than the flexibility of informal coordination.
In incident reviews, my attention first goes to individual decisions rather than system conditions.
I can support a subordinate's different approach without needing to make it my own.
Weak evidence concerns me even when the immediate consequences of an assumption seem limited.
Maintaining consistency in my decisions can feel more important than appearing flexible.
I am comfortable sacrificing a short-term objective to protect a more consequential future one.
I prefer to verify key assumptions personally before relying on a team-generated operational recommendation.
I can accept a calculated risk without needing every stakeholder to support my assessment.
When conditions change rapidly, I am inclined to simplify options rather than seek additional perspectives.
I give significant weight to low-probability events when their consequences could be severe.
I am reluctant to reopen a decision once the bridge or engine team has committed to it.
I distinguish between a failure of execution and a failure of judgment before assigning responsibility.
I prefer a decision process that can be explained afterwards over one that simply produces a quick result.
I am comfortable stating the limits of my expertise during a high-level operational discussion.
I sometimes regard repeated requests for data as unnecessary resistance to a decision.
I can revise a recommendation publicly without experiencing it as a loss of authority.
I am more comfortable accepting operational delays than accepting poorly defined exposure to risk.
I tend to trust a coherent narrative before checking whether contradictory data have been overlooked.
When several options meet minimum standards, I focus on their resilience to unexpected conditions.
I prefer to make my own risk trade-offs rather than follow a recommendation based on consensus.
I struggle to separate my confidence in a person from my confidence in their proposed action.
I actively look for evidence that could disprove my preferred operational interpretation.
I am willing to challenge an efficient practice when its controls depend too heavily on individual vigilance.
I feel pressure to offer a definitive answer even when uncertainty would be more accurate.
I consider the effect of a decision on the next watch or team, not only the present operation.
I find it easier to justify preventive action after a near miss than before one has occurred.
I can explain why a decision was reasonable without treating its success as proof it was correct.
When I inherit an operational plan, I examine its assumptions before accepting its conclusions.
I prefer to resolve disagreements about risk thresholds before operational pressure increases.
I sometimes give unusual incidents disproportionate weight because they are vivid in my memory.
I find it natural to distinguish reversible decisions from those with lasting consequences.
If a deadline is approaching, I tend to narrow consultation to protect the decision timetable.
I will reopen a settled issue if a credible junior officer identifies a new hazard.
I am more comfortable with decisions that distribute risk across several safeguards than rely on one strong safeguard.
I occasionally underestimate how my authority shapes the information that reaches me.
I can take ownership of an unpopular stop-work decision without seeking private reassurance afterwards.
I tend to regard an operational plan as provisional even after it has been formally approved.
I prefer explicit decision criteria when balancing safety, schedule and cost.
When a decision proves successful, I still examine whether unnecessary risks were accepted.
I am inclined to escalate an emerging concern before I can present a complete solution.
I sometimes equate thorough documentation with sound judgment more than I should.
I can tolerate a slower decision process when it produces substantially better challenge and review.
I question a recommendation more closely when it aligns too neatly with my initial preference.
I find it uncomfortable when accountability is shared across several departments.
I would rather expose uncertainty to senior management than offer confidence unsupported by evidence.
I can distinguish a genuine emergency from urgency created by commercial pressure.
I am cautious about changing a stable system solely to achieve marginal performance gains.
I prefer comparing several independent indicators before accepting a vessel's reported condition.
I sometimes interpret absence of recent failures as evidence that existing controls are sufficient.
I deliberately consider how a decision might appear to someone who must implement it.
I find it difficult to leave a material operational choice in another leader's hands.
I can pursue a well-supported minority view despite strong agreement among peers.
I favour plans with clear fallback options even when the primary approach is highly reliable.
I am willing to slow a meeting to clarify disagreements hidden beneath apparent consensus.
I sometimes give undue weight to the confidence with which a recommendation is delivered.
I am comfortable defining a decision point at which further information would no longer change my course.
I look for signs that routine success may be concealing an accumulating weakness.
I weigh the credibility of a source separately from the seniority of the person delivering it.
I feel more responsible for errors of action than for harm caused by delayed action.
When a plan begins to fail, I examine the underlying assumptions before increasing effort.
I prefer to agree on objective stopping criteria before commencing a demanding operation.
I can remain undecided temporarily without feeling that my leadership is being questioned.
I sometimes protect a previous decision by interpreting new information too favourably.
I think through how my current decision may constrain the vessel's later options.
I am more willing to question an optimistic forecast than a conservative one.
I regard challenge from technical specialists as a resource rather than a complication.
When outcomes are uncertain, I separate what can be controlled from what must be monitored.
I tend to seek a single accountable owner even for problems requiring cross-functional solutions.
I am prepared to revise a commercial commitment when operational assumptions no longer hold.
I find it difficult to make a final recommendation when several reasonable options remain.
I assess whether proposed efficiencies create hidden workload for another team or watch.
I prefer to preserve decision-making space instead of committing all resources early.
I sometimes value operational continuity more highly than the warning signs justify.
I can make a cautious decision without presenting caution as fear of responsibility.
I routinely consider whether established procedures still suit the conditions in which they are used.
I am inclined to ask what would change my mind before giving strong support to a proposal.
I place greater weight on the quality of a decision than on whether my prediction proves correct.
I can recognise when a technical problem has become an organisational decision problem.
I occasionally rely on seniority to settle debate when the evidence is inconclusive.
I remain willing to change course after communicating a firm position to external stakeholders.
I prefer clear assumptions and contingencies to detailed plans that appear certain.
I consider the cost of failing to act as carefully as the cost of taking action.
I find it easier to challenge another department's proposal than my own team's assumptions.
I can accept a recommendation that contradicts my experience when the supporting evidence is strong.
I pay attention to risks created by interactions between otherwise acceptable operational decisions.
I am prepared to admit that an apparently successful outcome involved more luck than sound judgment.
I maintain professional distance when familiarity might weaken the clarity of command.
When publicly challenged by an officer, I focus first on preserving clear authority.
Logical reasoning is usually more natural to me than emotional encouragement when influencing experienced people.
When team performance declines, I examine leadership conditions before individual shortcomings.
I sometimes withhold my preferred solution so senior officers must exercise independent judgment.
I become uneasy when delegated work succeeds through methods unlike my own.
I favour clear consequences over prolonged coaching when experienced officers repeatedly underperform.
I allow senior officers to resolve disagreements themselves unless operations are affected.
A serious lapse in judgment can permanently reduce how much autonomy I give an officer.
I adjust my leadership approach to different cultural expectations of authority.
Under pressure, I become more directive even with a highly capable team.
I judge leadership success partly by how well my team functions without me.
Repeated reassurance-seeking can make me question an officer's professional confidence.
I allow constructive disagreement to continue even when it slows a leadership meeting.
I sometimes overlook the emotional impact of an operationally sound decision.
I prefer communicating broad objectives rather than prescribing each step for senior officers.
I can overlook interpersonal difficulties when an officer delivers outstanding technical results.
I find developmental feedback easier than public recognition of exceptional performance.
Technical credibility feels more natural to me than relationship-building as a source of influence.
I accept short-term inefficiency when it provides meaningful development for future leaders.
I expect senior officers to surface concerns without requiring repeated invitations from me.
I sometimes take silence during a briefing as agreement more readily than I should.
I can change a previously assigned responsibility without implying that I distrust the officer.
I tend to address a weak professional relationship through clearer expectations rather than personal conversation.
I am comfortable having my own mistakes discussed as learning examples with the team.
I can distinguish respectful dissent from a challenge to my status.
When mentoring, I often feel tempted to supply the answer before the officer has reasoned it through.
I tailor the amount of supervision to the consequence of an error as well as the person's experience.
I notice when a technically strong officer is becoming isolated from colleagues.
I sometimes underestimate how strongly junior crew interpret my facial expression or tone.
I prefer a colleague who challenges me privately over one who questions my view in a group.
I am comfortable changing the usual speaking order to hear quieter team members first.
I give officers enough context to understand why an unpopular decision has been made.
I find it difficult to remain neutral when two valued colleagues are in conflict.
I recognise that competence in one situation does not automatically justify autonomy in another.
When an officer reports a mistake early, I focus on openness before discussing consequences.
I sometimes assume that capable people need less appreciation than inexperienced colleagues.
I adjust my language to avoid making technical expertise a barrier to participation.
I am prepared to defend a subordinate whose reasonable decision attracted unfair criticism.
I consider how rank differences may prevent important concerns from reaching me.
I sometimes prefer operational harmony over confronting a persistent behavioural problem.
I can deliver a firm instruction without communicating contempt or frustration.
I encourage specialists from different departments to challenge one another's assumptions.
I find it uncomfortable when an officer becomes more knowledgeable than I am in a key area.
I ask for feedback on the effect of my leadership, not only on work outcomes.
I naturally become more protective of control when I doubt the cohesion of a team.
I distinguish deliberate non-compliance from misunderstanding before deciding how to respond.
I sometimes rely on the same dependable officers instead of developing less confident team members.
I value an officer who raises an inconvenient concern as much as one who executes a plan smoothly.
I recognise when an efficient command style is discouraging initiative.
I consider personal circumstances when interpreting a sudden change in an officer's behaviour.
I am comfortable acknowledging good ideas from crew who hold less senior roles.
I sometimes give stronger feedback about failures than about behaviours worth repeating.
I can maintain fairness when an officer's communication style differs from my own.
I give teams the freedom to question how a result should be achieved within agreed controls.
I feel more comfortable coaching privately than inviting peers to offer feedback to each other.
I notice when my presence changes the openness of a discussion.
I encourage officers to explain their reasoning rather than merely report completed actions.
I can support an unpopular team member when their professional concern is valid.
I sometimes confuse fast agreement with strong commitment from the team.
I prefer developing a successor who will challenge my habits rather than replicate them.
I give clear boundaries before delegating a decision with significant operational consequences.
I tend to interpret a cautious officer's repeated questions as reluctance to take ownership.
I can maintain respect for someone while imposing a formal performance consequence.
I invite feedback from crew who have previously disagreed with me.
I am more comfortable with formal reporting lines than informal cross-rank problem-solving.
I recognise when instructions appear clear to me but leave others uncertain about priorities.
I sometimes expect officers to adapt to my communication style more than I adapt to theirs.
I assess whether my interventions are building confidence or creating dependence.
I know when to move a difficult personal discussion away from a group setting.
I openly discuss competing priorities so the team understands the basis of trade-offs.
I can delegate visible leadership opportunities without feeling less influential.
I become frustrated when colleagues need emotional reassurance during a technically demanding operation.
I use questions to uncover disagreement rather than asking only whether everyone understands.
I treat concerns raised near the end of an operation as seriously as those raised at the beginning.
I sometimes continue to supervise an officer closely after they have demonstrated sufficient independence.
I can give direct corrective feedback while preserving an individual's dignity.
I notice when culturally different forms of deference are masking uncertainty.
I am willing to revisit how responsibilities are distributed when a team becomes overloaded.
I can separate personal loyalty from my evaluation of professional performance.
I prefer rewarding consistent team contribution over celebrating a single exceptional individual.
I sometimes give more authority to confident communicators than to equally capable quiet colleagues.
I encourage senior officers to identify weaknesses in the way I set priorities.
I remain receptive when an officer questions whether my instruction is practical in current conditions.
I recognise that a highly efficient crew may still have unresolved trust problems.
I sometimes assume that a person's rank guarantees their ability to handle conflict.
I can admit to a team that my communication contributed to a misunderstanding.
I intervene when humour or informal habits undermine someone's willingness to speak up.
I prefer developing shared judgment within a team over requiring identical decisions from everyone.
I am willing to rotate responsibilities even when the arrangement temporarily reduces efficiency.
I recognise when my strongest performers are carrying an unsustainable share of the workload.
I find it harder to acknowledge strong ideas when they are presented confrontationally.
I create opportunities for junior crew to contribute before senior voices dominate a discussion.
I can give an officer clear accountability without isolating them when a problem arises.
I sometimes focus on whether an instruction was followed more than whether it was understood.
I make time to understand friction between shipboard and shore-based teams before attributing blame.
I can adjust the balance of consultation and direction without confusing the team.
I encourage a departing team member to share concerns they may have hesitated to raise earlier.
I am willing to share credit for results even when I initiated the successful approach.
I regard the team's willingness to challenge me as one indicator of my leadership effectiveness.
When several problems emerge together, I become more task-focused than consultative.
I struggle to disengage mentally from unresolved work after formally handing it over.
I first examine the limitations of a new procedure before considering its potential benefits.
I can remain receptive to criticism from someone with much less experience.
Under sustained pressure, I reduce informal communication and focus on essential matters.
I am comfortable admitting uncertainty when the team expects immediate reassurance.
Repeated challenges to my judgment sometimes feel like a lack of confidence in my leadership.
I need to understand the strategic reason for a major change before fully committing to it.
I can appear composed even when I am experiencing considerable internal concern.
After setbacks, I focus on causal decisions before processing their emotional impact.
I find it difficult to remain patient with people who respond to pressure differently from me.
I will reconsider a long-held belief when credible evidence conflicts with my experience.
I sometimes underestimate the effect of prolonged responsibility on my judgment.
When expectations are ambiguous, I prefer discretion to seeking repeated clarification.
I can express disagreement with management when I believe risk is unacceptable.
Technological change feels easier for me than shifts in organisational culture.
When stakeholder demands conflict, I try to preserve relationships before stating a firm position.
I become highly self-critical when results fall short of my own standards.
I can change a leadership method that previously served me well but is now less effective.
I remain concerned about weak safeguards even when operational performance looks satisfactory.
I can maintain my usual standards of courtesy when I am mentally exhausted.
I sometimes treat rest as less important than resolving a difficult operational problem.
I accept new evidence more readily when it does not call my earlier decisions into question.
I find it useful to distinguish genuine urgency from anxiety spreading through a team.
I can acknowledge emotional strain without feeling it undermines my professional authority.
When circumstances disrupt a carefully prepared plan, I tend to recover my focus quickly.
I sometimes suppress concerns to avoid appearing uncertain in front of senior colleagues.
I am willing to test a new approach on a limited scale before making a full commitment.
I can accept that a colleague's different response to stress may still be effective.
I find it harder to adapt when change is introduced without meaningful consultation.
I recognise when confidence in my ability is starting to become overconfidence.
I remain courteous when I believe another person's mistake has created avoidable pressure.
I sometimes continue working past the point at which my concentration is declining.
I am comfortable seeking advice from someone outside my normal professional circle.
I can separate criticism of my decisions from criticism of my character.
When an operational change causes temporary confusion, I remain willing to support its longer-term purpose.
I find it difficult to tolerate uncertainty when other people seem more relaxed about it.
I can tell the difference between emotional composure and emotional suppression in myself.
I am prepared to report a concern even when it may reflect poorly on my own team.
I am more likely to change my views gradually than after a single compelling discussion.
I can remain effective when my preferred way of working is unavailable.
I sometimes become impatient when safety discussions revisit a risk I consider settled.
I can give a balanced account of my own contribution to an unsuccessful outcome.
I find it natural to acknowledge when sustained stress is affecting my sleep or concentration.
I remain open to change when it comes from a department with which I often disagree.
I can handle a reduction in my authority without interpreting it as a loss of professional worth.
I sometimes use additional work as a way of avoiding a difficult personal conversation.
I maintain professional standards even when I believe a requirement is inefficient.
I can resist pressure to present a more favourable account of events than the evidence supports.
I recover my confidence after a setback without dismissing the lessons it revealed.
I tend to prefer familiar routines when personal pressure outside work is increasing.
I can tolerate being temporarily less competent while learning an unfamiliar system.
I find it difficult to admit that fatigue has affected my decisions.
I am willing to communicate bad news before I can explain every contributing factor.
I can remain curious about a proposal that initially threatens my established responsibilities.
I sometimes rely on emotional detachment so heavily that colleagues experience me as distant.
I understand that an apparently resilient colleague may still need support.
I prefer to prepare for change by identifying what must remain stable.
I can disagree firmly without allowing frustration to influence my treatment of others.
I am inclined to keep personal worries private even when they begin affecting my leadership.
I can adapt after a change in leadership without repeatedly comparing it with the previous arrangement.
I remain willing to review my conduct after an incident, even when I followed the procedure.
I sometimes respond to uncertainty by asking for more control over details than I need.
I can maintain ethical boundaries when a short-term exception would be difficult to detect.
I find it easier to address technical uncertainty than interpersonal uncertainty.
I consider whether my normal stress response creates unintended pressure for others.
I can change my mind without needing colleagues to acknowledge that my earlier view was reasonable.
I sometimes overcommit because I feel personally responsible for every important result.
I can uphold an unpopular standard without becoming resentful toward those who challenge it.
I adapt more easily when I can contribute to the design of a change.
I recognise when determination is becoming an obstacle to reassessing my approach.
I can openly acknowledge a decision that conflicts with my previous public position.
I find it difficult to stop thinking about a professional disagreement after it has been resolved.
I can remain constructive when constraints prevent me from achieving my preferred standard.
I am prepared to challenge misleading reporting even if the immediate outcome benefits my department.
I sometimes confuse not showing emotion with managing emotion effectively.
I am willing to revise a routine after learning from another vessel's experience.
I can accept temporary ambiguity in my role during a major organisational transition.
I sometimes become more critical of others when I am under prolonged pressure.
I can hold myself accountable without turning every mistake into a personal failure.
I prefer to assess the practical effect of a new policy rather than judge it by who proposed it.
I can identify when fear of reputational damage is influencing my recommendations.
I sometimes dismiss emerging concerns because I have handled similar problems before.
I am comfortable asking for a pause when pressure is beginning to impair the quality of discussion.
I maintain the same reporting standards when a near miss causes no immediate harm.
I can adapt my routines when a team needs a different form of support.
I find it difficult to disengage from a problem when someone else is taking an approach I would not choose.
I can discuss errors without immediately searching for a person to blame.
I am willing to correct inaccurate records even when the correction may attract scrutiny.
I sometimes resist change primarily because it makes my experience feel less relevant.
I can recognise when a colleague's strong reaction signals a concern worth exploring.
I recover from an unexpected operational setback without rushing into compensating actions.
I prefer honest uncertainty over confident messages that could create false reassurance.
I can maintain sound boundaries between professional responsibility and personal identity.
I sometimes postpone difficult ethical conversations in the hope that circumstances will resolve them.
I remain open to feedback after a successful operation, not only after a failure.
I can sustain respectful relationships with people whose professional values differ from mine.
I resist the temptation to redefine an agreed standard merely to make performance appear acceptable.
I can reassess my coping methods when an extended period of pressure makes them less effective.
I remain willing to learn from critical feedback even when its delivery feels unfair.
